items.title: A Less-Than-Satisfying End to a Landmark Trump II Legal Battle
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
I suspect many of you thought that Kilmar Abrego Garcia had prevailed in court long ago and may have been surprised to see him self-deport to Spain overnight. He reportedly hasn’t made a decision about his ultimate destination.

But while the man subjected to a sustained campaign of brutalization by the Trump administrations had won landmark court cases, the law still gave the government enormous power over his ultimate fate — giving him few good choices.

For many months now, Abrego Garcia had been trying to leave the country on his own, but the Trump administration had refused to allow it. It’s not clear what changed the equation for the administration, but by allowing him to leave now it does avoid having appeals courts weigh in on some of its most egregious conduct over the past two years.

Let me briefly orient you, and then we’ll zoom back out to the big picture.

There were essentially three Abrego Garcia cases, and he won all three:

  1. Wrongful deportation to El Salvador: Abrego Garcia was removed to CECOT in his home country the same March 2025 weekend as the Alien Enemies Act deportations in violation of an immigration judge’s order that barred his removal because of his fears of persecution and torture. He challenged his removal and took the case all the way to the Supreme Court, which, in a landmark ruling, ordered the Trump administration to “facilitate” his return.

  2. Vindictive criminal prosecution: Under order from the Supreme Court to facilitate Abrego Garcia’s return, the Trump DOJ indicted him on trumped-up human trafficking charges in Tennessee. When he returned to the United States, he was immediately put in federal custody on the criminal charges. He successfully challenged his prosecution as a vindictive response to his winning the civil case. The Trump DOJ’s appeal of that ruling was still pending, and just yesterday the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals scheduled oral arguments in the appeal for Feb. 24, 2027.

  3. : As its criminal case against Abrego Garcia was falling apart, the Trump administration began threatening to deport him to a series of African countries to which he had no ties even though Costa Rica came forward to say that it would take him. Abrego Garcia succeeded in winning release from custody after it became clear that the Trump administration was using the hollow threat of imminent third-country deportation to keep him detained. The Trump DOJ’s appeal of that ruling was still pending before the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals.

Abrego Garcia’s expressed willingness to leave the country voluntarily had meant that for months there was an available exit ramp for the Trump administration if it chose to take it. Repeated delays agreed to by the parties in both of the pending appeals hinted that something might be in the works, but news of the arrangement only emerged last evening as Abrego Garcia was set to fly out of Dulles.

With Abrego Garcia safely in Spain this morning, U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis of Maryland — who did yeoman’s work overseeing both the civil cases — issued an order dissolving the remaining injunctions, ruling on the remaining motions, and closing the case. The two pending appeals and the criminal case will presumably be closed now, too.

Interestingly, Judge Xinis also unsealed a Nov. 20 order that now reveals what was in the works. The Nov. 20 order came after Judge Xinis engaged in a “consultation with the parties” on Oct. 6, an event that was not publicly listed on the court docket. Her subsequent order set the conditions of Abrego Garcia’s departure, including the departure date of Nov. 24. It also removed any remaining obstacles to his departure, including ordering his ankle monitor removed before he boarded the airplane, prohibiting the government from interfering with his departure or from treating it as a violation of any condition of his release.

The Trump administration took one last parting shot at Abrego Garcia, re-upping its 20-month campaign of defaming and dehumanizing him:

There remains one important bit of unfinished business. Judge Xinis still has a potential contempt of court inquiry pending into the conduct of the Trump DOJ and DHS from the first civil case. She had prioritized the substance of the legal challenges by Abrego Garcia but presumably can now return to that unresolved matter.

While Abrego Garcia’s self-deportation may feel like an unsatisfactory conclusion to this saga, this has been the best plausible outcome for him for some time. It took extraordinary work from his legal teams in both the civil and criminal cases. It took bold and determined federal judges in Maryland and Tennessee. It took appeals courts having the backs of district judges.

In the Trump II era, wins can be hard to come by, and they may not look as pretty and clear-cut as our pre-Trump selves would have wanted. But there’s a danger that we can redefine wins out of existence by setting the bar too high. This was a huge win for Abrego Garcia and his legal team while still being an abomination by the Trump administration.

“For years, the Administration has treated the weaponization of law enforcement like a horror movie villain coming for them. Now the threat is finally real. Only the call is coming from inside the house—the White House. Perhaps, less time on the pool and more on reflecting.”—U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui of D.C., in a blistering opinion dismissing the politicized prosecution of veteran FBI agents Bradley Benavides and Nikki Cole Floris

The Trump DOJ was forced to file an admission of error in federal court after it falsely described the legal position taken by the House general counsel on the FBI search of the D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN).

“The United States apologizes for this inadvertent misunderstanding,” prosecutors from U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office said in the filing.

Far from hanging Omar out to dry, the House’s top lawyer took a much more muted position than the Trump DOJ had previously conveyed to U.S. District Judge James Boasberg.

The new filing includes a copy of the October email response from House general counsel Matthew Berry to Trent McCotter, who is now the acting deputy attorney general. In addition to revealong McCotter’s role in the error, it shows the vindictive investigation of Omar being directed by the highest levels of the Trump DOJ.

Dems Win at Least 259 House Seats

The AP finally called the TN-04 race for Democrat Victoria Broderick, who knocks off incumbent Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R), who had conceded days ago.

In the Alaska Senate, incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) finally conceded to Democrat Mary Peltola.

As a tribute to my late friend Paul Johnson, I am once again sharing his beloved turkey gumbo recipe. Friends don’t let friends waste a good roast turkey carcass.

See you back here Monday.

items.title: A Culture of Impunity Unites Trump and Tech Oligarchs
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Blanche Reportedly Cleared Huang

But it manages to be all of those things and also a new and stunning example of the culture of impunity for the techno-authoritarian oligarchy that was heralded by President Trump’s re-election. Trump and the tech billionaires sustain and reinforce each other’s predilections for an accountability free-zone in which they can operate freely, avoid legal consequences, pay low taxes, enjoy dalliances with subordinates, and cosplay as masters of the universe.

President Trump’s direct involvement in the restoration of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia is simply without precedent. Trump not only called into the meeting of the Nvidia board and all but demanded (on what terms we do not know yet) that it reinstate Huang despite his serial lying to his own directors, but he essentially leaked the news yesterday to Liz Landers of PBS before the markets opened. The opportunities for corruption around that one bit of insider information could be a whole scandal of its own.

But Trump did not proceed — and may not have proceeded — without the clean bill of health that Huang received from Attorney General Todd Blanche, according to the WSJ:

Over the weekend, Attorney General Todd Blanche presented an opening. The nation’s top law enforcement officer informed Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Saturday that Huang wasn’t the target or the subject of any Justice Department investigation, adding that the department had no evidence to suggest that he had broken laws or was a national security risk, according to U.S. officials.

That by itself is an astounding position for the attorney general to take, given the reported intelligence concerns around Huang’s honeypot vulnerability, the national security concerns around the alleged transshipment of Nvidia chips to China in violation of export restrictions, and the attorney general’s dual role in law enforcement and counterintelligence.

We may never know if what Blanche told Trump and Vance was literally true or what he thought they wanted to hear or what they told him they wanted to hear — or was made true by Trump ordering it to be so. It was not apparently the first time Trump has come to the rescue of a tech billionaire.

Even as the news of Huang’s reinstatement was breaking, Trump was bragging on national TV about previously protecting Elon Musk during Trump I from unspecified accountability. It is similarly unclear whether this is a truthful recounting of an actual episode or something Trump needed or wanted to be true:

I often think back to the Solyndra “scandal.” If you don’t remember, Republicans tried to made the collapse of the solar panel maker (which had received loan guarantees from the Obama administration) the signature scandal of Obama’s first term and derail his 2012 re-election. It was a byword for scandal before Benghazi. For a while, it injected “crony capitalism” into the political vernacular. It was, in Republican’s telling, everything wrong with the intersection of government and industry. And it was all bullshit.

Like so much else about modern Republicanism, Solyndra was a projection. It presaged the Trump con of accusing Democrats of the precise corrupt thing he was already doing or would later go on to do. Even if everything about the made-up Solyndra scandal had turned out to be true (and, again, it wasn’t), it would be massively dwarfed by the Nvidia scandal — and a few dozen other similar Trump II depredations which has the WSJ warning about “state capitalism.”

Coming into Trump II, one of the big unknowns was whether corporate America would hold the line or be coopted by the regime. We now know how quickly some companies capitulated, and how far-reaching Trump’s effort would go to cement his political power by interweaving it with direct economic control over companies and industries.

I was hopeful that the midterm election shellacking marked the high water mark for Trump’s crony capitalism. But now Jensen Huang is back, and we’re in for at least another two years of this.

Was Alice Huang Really a ‘Spy’?

Interviews with current and former U.S. intelligence officials, lawmakers and China analysts suggest the spy-or-not-a-spy question misses a broader point. The greater challenge, they say, is that China’s intelligence services have grown so expansive and opportunistic under Xi that the line between a recruited agent and an unwitting asset has blurred—making it harder to assess the damage and easier to dismiss the threat.

Raskin Targets Don Jr.’s Biz Interests

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD), the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee, is demanding information from four companies that reportedly saw big investments from Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital Management, and experienced favorable federal government actions.

The companies and the actions that Raskin is interested in:

  • : The “nascent” defense contractor received almost a billion dollars in military contracts under Trump II.

  • : The vape company benefited from FDA authorization and approval for e-cigarette products.

  • : The Commodity Futures Trading Commission and DOJ closed investigations of the prediction market company last year, and CFTC cleared the way for it to acquire a derivatives exchange.

  • : The online gun retailer benefitted from an ATF proposed rule that would make online firearm purchasing easier.

Polygraphs for Trump Appointees at DOJ?

Attorney General Todd Blanche’s chief of staff warned top DOJ political appointees that they may be polygraphed to determine who’s been leaking to the press, Bloomberg reports.

Omar Hung Out To Dry by House Counsel

U.S. District Judge James Boasberg of D.C. ordered the unsealing of heavily redacted court filings surrounding the FBI search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s D.C. home. Among the revelations in the unsealed filing (which did not include the search warrant itself):

  • Prosecutors are reaching all the way back to 1980 in search of evidence that Omar, 44, has “committed [redacted] crimes over decades—beginning long before she was ever in Congress.”

  • Ahead of the search, U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh ordered prosecutors to institute safeguards to prevent her legislative work from being swept up in the search, in violation of the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause, and expressed frustration that they didn’t initially take his concerns seriously.

  • Sharbaugh apparently ordered prosecutors to notify House General Counsel Matthew Berry before conducting the search, but prosecutors reported that he “refused to be involved” and took the position that Speech or Debate Clause protections “do not extend to a Member’s private residence.”

The House general counsel seemingly failing to come to Omar’s defense is a startling departure under Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) from the House’s usual reflexive defense of its institutional interests.

items.title: White House Plots Grand Cover-up of Trump II Corruption and Lawlessness
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
The Mother of All Cover-Ups

With so much to hide, the Trump White House is running scared from oversight by the incoming Democratic Congress, and it shows in the form of performative preemptive resistance that it hopes will run out the clock on the Trump II presidency.

It’s a cover-up on a scale never before witnessed in American history, backstopped by a Justice Department under the thumb of the Trump White House that will never prosecute and a Supreme Court that granted wide-ranging presidential immunity.

On the heels of the mockable threats to prosecute members of Congress for congressing come two new moves by the White House to interpose itself between Congress and potential witnesses to Trump II wrongdoing. The first was a directive from new Trump Chief of Staff Stephen Miller that federal government employees can’t testify to Congress without pre-approval from the White House.

Then on Friday came a new executive order to try to keep government contractors from talking to congressional investigators. Titled “Protecting the Executive’s Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting,” the new EO purports to require contractors to notify the White House of “any pending or future congressional request.”

Perhaps most importantly, the EO attempts to smother congressional oversight under a blanket of executive privilege. It purports to require government contractors to “abide by any instructions received from the White House and contracting agency related to the withholding of communications that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege.”

As we discussed here last week, government contractors, subcontractors, vendors, and suppliers are a prime target for congressional oversight — a way around the White House’s challenges to congressional subpoenas and spurious executive privilege claims. Recognizing that vulnerability, the Trump White House is now trying to cow government contractors into either not cooperating or slow-rolling their cooperation with Congress — or at the very least to coerce them into giving the White House a heads up on congressional inquiries.

As Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck observes, the Miller directive and new EO work together to ensure “that nothing reaches Congress until the White House clears it. That isn’t the law, and it has never been executive branch practice during any prior administration. As with so many other things these days, we’re in uncharted territory on the separation of powers arguments.”

We’re starting to test the logical extremes of the unitary executive theory and whether executive privilege shields the entire executive branch from routine congressional oversight.

A separate “Fact Sheet” issued by the White House positions the EO as protection against “congressional overreach” — which, it needs to be said, hasn’t even happened since the new Congress hasn’t been sworn in yet. It’s couched in terms of protecting “Americans’ confidential information” from “unauthorized disclosure” to “unauthorized third parties,” including “members of Congress.”

To give the EO some teeth, it explicitly threatens government contractors, as former U.S. Attorney Joyce Vance notes:

[T]he administration puts the full weight of economic blackmail behind its plan for keeping Congress in the dark about what it’s been up to. The punishment for contractors that respond to Congress’ lawful demands without executive branch approval includes termination or cancellation of contracts and blackslisting (called debarment) of contractors so they can no longer do any work with the federal government.

While there’s an almost comical level of gamesmanship and trolling in trying to shut down all avenues to congressional oversight, it’s ultimately a quite serious attempt to cover up the sins of the first two years of Trump’s second term, when the GOP Congress abdicated its constitutional oversight responsibilities.

Running out the clock is part of the cover-up. Every skirmish — whether directly between Congress and the White House or indirectly between the White House and third party witnesses who work for the government or government contractors — delays the ultimate reckoning for the depredations of the Trump II presidency.

Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC), an 11-term incumbent, has lost her re-election bid following a recount. The race in the NC-05 was finally called over the weekend, and Foxx conceded to her Democratic challenger, Chuck Hubbard.

Things That Make You Go, Hmmm …

Outgoing Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-NY) and her family sold the D.C. rowhouse where she has lived while in Congress to a mystery buyer in June for $900,000 over the list price, the WaPo reports.

The Trump DOJ continues to “investigate” the 2020 presidential election.

On Friday, the FBI conducted a two-hours-plus interview of Richard Barron, the former elections director for Fulton County, Georgia, the NYT reports: “In attendance were two F.B.I. agents and two federal prosecutors, including Dan Bishop, a former congressman from North Carolina and Trump loyalist who was appointed in April as the Justice Department’s top election fraud prosecutor, Mr. Barron said.”

Barron agreed to the do the interview voluntarily and not under subpoena, he said.

In recent days, federal agents have contacted two other Fulton County officials who worked on the 2020 election, according to the NYT: Nadine Williams, who is now the head of the county’s elections division, and Ralph Jones, who was the county’s voter registration chief.

  • : U.S. District Judge April Perry will herself investigate whether the Trump DOJ lied to her about the Broadview 6 prosecution, rejecting a last-minute bid by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward for her to appoint a special master to do the work. In denying Woodward’s motion on Friday, Judge Perry wrote:

The Government has known for more than five months that the Court planned to hold a hearing regarding the conduct of the federal prosecutors in this matter, and for more than three months that potentially privileged communications would be at issue during that hearing.Despite this, the Government waited until 6:50 p.m. the night before potentially privileged materials would be tendered to the Court to file its motion. The request is therefore untimely. Moreover, the substance of the motion reflects a basic misapprehension about what a special master does.

  • : In a memo last week, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter urged Trump DOJ employees not to cite American Bar Association materials, according to Bloomberg, which obtained a copy of the memo. “Department reliance on ABA materials risks legitimizing the ABA and its positions,” McCotter wrote.

The Nvidia board has reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, saying it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” that made it “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Huang’s reinstatement came after President Trump posted Sunday night on social media that he hoped the board would rehire Huang.

Treating Canada Like a Punching Bag

In a classified memo last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth imposed new restrictions on the U.S.-Canada defense relationship, including limiting social engagements between American and Canadian service members, such as attending conferences or academic events, the WaPo reports.

A man carelessly working on his laptop on the DC Metro train revealed a draft plan for executive firings and sweeping changes at the National Museum of American History, ProPublica reports.

items.title: Tillis Knifes Controversial Trump Nominee for GAO
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Time Is Running Out on the Ueland Nom

Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) appears poised to effectively kill the nomination of White House aide Eric Ueland to a 15-year term as head of the Government Accountability Office.

Overnight, Tillis told Politico that he will block the Ueland nomination from being included in a package of presidential nominations the Senate will vote to confirm next month before the clock runs out on the GOP majority.

“I’ve already issued a presumptive hold if it comes out of committee,” Tillis said in an interview last night. “I won’t allow him to go through en bloc.”

The showdown over the lame-duck attempt to install Ueland as comptroller general of the United States has pitted a White House testing the new limits of its powers after a midterm shellacking against a shell-shocked GOP-controlled Senate that has endured two years of Trump humiliations and encroachments on its power. (Democrats in the minority are mostly bystanders to this mini-saga, though they have stirred the pot to the extent possible.)

Ueland’s nomination was like throwing gas on a smoldering fire. He is the deputy director of the White House Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the radical who spearheaded Trump’s Project 2025 agenda. No one more than Vought has sought to erode Congress’ Article I powers and vest them in the executive branch. No one has done more to bypass, repudiate, and weaken Congress’ power of the purse.

Under the circumstances, putting Ueland in charge of the GAO was a fox-guarding-the-henhouse move. Vought’s OMB has been engaged in a running gun battle with the GAO over the Impoundment Control Act, which only the comptroller general can sue to enforce. The nomination of Ueland was a thumb in the eye of Republicans to see how much more abuse they’d willingly take from Trump even after he cost them their majorities in both chambers.

It also highlighted the structural flaw of having the GAO serve as a creature of the legislative branch, but with its head appointed by the president. The White House had stonewalled the nominating of a new comptroller general for months, only to pivot to Ueland this week in a last-minute post-election move that left no time for consultation or vetting by the 10-member bipartisan, bicameral congressional commission that recommends candidates to the White House.

Senate rules are often the enemy of clarity, making it hard to declare outright that the Ueland nomination is dead. But Tillis’ move to block the nomination at this phase creates two difficult to surmount obstacles: It leaves little time for Republicans to get the nomination through on its own, and it robs Ueland of the protection of being in a package that senators have to take or leave as a whole.

There’s also no real reason to think Tillis — who didn’t seek re-election because he was almost certain to lose in the GOP primary without Trump’s support — wouldn’t put a hold on the nomination again if it came back up on its own. This appears to have been the easiest and quickest way for Tillis to knife the nomination for good but stay tuned.

WATCH: The Three Horseman of the Trump II Apocalypse

Almost exactly two years ago, just after the 2024 election, I wrote a post on “The Three Horsemen Of The Trump II Apocalypse” that framed the central themes of the incoming presidency as retribution, corruption, and destruction.

I went on the TPM Social Club podcast to talk about how that framing has fared, this week’s debut of Unsanctioned, and whole bunch of other stuff. Give it a listen:

The Destruction: Ph.D. Edition

The overall number of new full-time doctoral students in the sciences at U.S. universities fell 10% in the first year of Trump II, according to a NYT analysis. Among top-tier research schools, the decline was 11%, and three-quarters of that decline was driven by plummeting enrollment among international students.

The Retribution: Mar-a-Lago Edition

Bloomberg: “The Justice Department has deployed top Los Angeles prosecutor Bill Essayli to Miami for a special assignment to try probing the people involved in searching Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence in 2022, said three people familiar with the situation.”

Jan. 6 Never Ends: Supercut Edition

BREAKING: Judge Blocks Trump Arch

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Alexandria, Virginia, just issued an oral preliminary injunction from the bench against Trump’s triumphal arch.

Secretary Rollins Violated Constitution With Christmas and Easter Emails

A federal judge in California ruled yesterday that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins violated the First Amendment’s Establishment Clause when she sent overtly religious Christmas and Easter emails to all department employees.

Great Read on Grand Theft Auto VI

I’m not now and never really have been a gamer, but I’ve been fascinated by the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. I know I’ve already lost a few of you, but there’s a great read coming here in a moment so hang in there.

Just to give fellow non-gamers some sense of the scale of the enterprise: GTA VI cost about $1.4 billion to develop and was projected to reach $3.3 billion in sales in its first week, according to the WSJ. Then on the first day of release yesterday, it hit an estimated $2.36 billion in sales, Reuters reports.

For a non-gamer like me trying to understand this as an entertainment business and cultural phenomenon, it was helpful to see the projected sales compared to more familiar events like the 2024 Olympics, Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour, and Hamilton Broadway sales :

Now to the fun part. Allowed pre-release access under an NDA, Joseph Bernstein has written a tour de force on GTA VI for the NYT Mag. I don’t want to spoil it for you, but if you want a super smart read that bridges the gap for non-gamers, I highly recommend it.

If you’re still not convinced, he describes the satirical elements of the game in a way that sounds like a post-apocalyptic virtual world that Barbara Ehrenreich would recognize, as if “Nickel and Dimed” married “Miami Vice” and gave birth to the Trump era. Enjoy!

items.title: Cornyn Nixes Judgeship for OLC Head After Shouting Match With Ted Cruz
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Author of Boat Strike Memo Is From Ohio

Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) appears to have killed the judicial nomination of T. Elliot Gaiser, the 37-year-old head of the Office of Legal Counsel at the Trump DOJ who authored legal justifications for some of the administration’s most egregious extralegal conduct, including the lawless boat strike campaign.

“He’s not from Texas. He hasn’t been vetted. And this is a lifetime job, and there’s better qualified people to hold that job,” Cornyn told the AP. “This is part, of course, of the constitutional responsibility of senators in the Senate to provide advice and consent. But it’s hard to provide advice and consent when there’s zero consultation, which happened in that case.”

Gaiser did not appear on the confirmation hearing yesterday for a batch of Trump judicial nominees (who as a group refused to say that the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021). Cornyn’s leverage over the nomination comes from the Senate’s “blue-slip” tradition, still honored by Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Charles Grassley (R-IA), of not moving judicial nominations without the approval of home state senators.

Cornyn’s public break with the administration came after he and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) got into a loud argument on the Senate floor Tuesday over the Gaiser nomination. The whole imbroglio is heavily colored by Cornyn losing re-election in the GOP primary after Trump endorsed his opponent Ken Paxton, who went on to lose the general election that Cornyn his convinced he himself would have won.

Things continued to spill out in public on Wednesday with the Justice Department tacking a whack at Cornyn: “It is deeply disappointing that Senator Cornyn would choose political obstruction over advancing a highly qualified nominee.”

Cruz put out his own statement warning that there’s not time to confirm anyone else to the vacant judgeship: “If the Senate Judiciary Committee does not move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay the price because it will effectively give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity,” Cruz said. “That would be a tragedy.”

Another outgoing GOP senator primaried by President Trump got a measure of revenge.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), the chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, abruptly cancelled a committee vote on the nomination of Jim O’Neill to lead the National Science Foundation.

O’Neill previously worked in multiple roles at the Department of Health and Human Services under Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from Secretary Kennedy,” said Cassidy, who indicated that some other members of the committee shared his concerns.

Cassidy’s move effectively scuttled the nomination.

Election 2026 By the Numbers

A few new data points as the vote-counting nears an end:

  • Democrats lead in the national House vote has expanded to 14-percentage points, the largest margin by either party since Democrats romped by 16.6 points in the 1974 post-Watergate election.

  • Democrats have won at least 257 House seats, with six races still uncalled by the AP.

  • At least 109 House seats will be held by freshman, the most since at least 1998.

  • : Allies have launched Team Pete PAC to back another presidential run by the former secretary of transportation. (Politico)

  • : The Democratic senator from Arizona is bringing longtime aide Emma Brown back into the fold as he considers a White House run. (Politico)

  • : “Looking at it right now, it’s absolutely a savagely brutal map,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH), the incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. (Politico)

The Dog That’s Obviously Not Barking

After the Trump DOJ brought a flurry of noncitizen voting cases right before the election — touting them with press releases, press conferences, and mug shots — it has brought only one new noncitizen voting case since the Nov. 3 election, the WaPo reports.

The Corruption: IRS Edition

ProPublica reports on under-the-radar Trump administration settlement of a claims against the IRS for leaking taxpayer info.

It recalls Trump’s own settlement with the IRS and the planned creation of $1.776 billion slush fund.

But it’s not Trump this time.

It’s the longtime golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley.

And despite the settlement, the case isn’t over yet.

Two other people connected to Trump properties are trying to get in on the action: a retired accountant at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley and a former lifeguard at the Trump golf club in Westchester County, New York.

  • Colorado Public Radio: In a new contempt of court ruling, U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney excoriated ICE for repeatedly violating court orders with its policy of immediately re-detaining immigrants after they had been ordered to be released from detention. But Sweeney declined to take any further action, ruling that ICE officials had cured the contempt of court by ceasing the practice at issue.

  • Greg Sargent: ICE has $91 billion of no-strings-attached funding to spend on deportations between now and the end of Trump’s second term.

  • Nicholas Kristof: Trump ‘Disappeared’ Them in 2025. I Found Them, Locked Up and Famished.

Bo French Booted From Country Club

Republican Bo French’s racist (and losing) campaign for Texas Railroad Commission has cost him his membership in the River Crest Country Club in Fort Worth. The country club’s board of directors booted him after he refused to resign his membership.

Thanks For All the AI Feedback!

I received quite a rich and varied response to my question yesterday about which AI tools you’ve found to be useful. Many thanks for taking the time to email.

First off, y’all are awesome. You’re a remarkable cross section of creatives and what we now call “knowledge workers” (I hate that term): scientists, engineers, teachers, musicians, writers, attorneys, CEOs, founders, environmental consultants, and IT experts — many of whom are also doing side gigs for fun. Those of you who purport to be retired are busy af, serving on boards and volunteering and running your own pet projects.

You’ve discovered uses for AI that range from the practical to the whimsical to the sublime. This initial sampling of reader responses are personal and side projects uses that delighted me:

TPM Reader : “I manage my own forested acreage in Washington State for enjoyment, health, and minor income. I was kind of at a point where I wanted to get more focused, more deliberate, and more comprehensive in my management planning and use of my time and labor. My son suggested I get a monthly ChatGPT account to facilitate that. The results have been dazzling.”

TPM Reader : “It helped me build two ten foot bird feeder poles with offset arms to stop raccoons and squirrels.”

TPM Reader : “Because of ChatGPT I have been able to do a pet project, a searchable index of historic cookbooks in the public domain.”

items.title: A Peek at What We Still Don’t Know About the Worst of Trump II … So Far
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Trump Sicced the IRS on Protesters

I hinted in yesterday’s Unsanctioned that one of the major benefits of Congress reviving its oversight powers under new Democratic majorities will be to provide a fuller accounting of what’s already happened in the first two years of Trump II.

As bad as it’s been on the retribution, corruption, and destruction fronts, we only know a fraction of what’s really gone down. Vigorous congressional oversight — absent under the GOP majorities — promises to gives us a clearer picture of the worst of the Trump II depredations, like the mass deportation operation, and uncover wrongdoing we don’t even know about yet.

We get a new peek today at what that might look like in a NYT story that shows the IRS directly involved in targeting left-wing political groups in the aftermath of the assassination of Charlie Kirk. The IRS “initiated at least four criminal investigations” into as-yet-unidentified left-wing groups, according to a portion of an internal memo obtained by the NYT.

“The memo describes the work done by a group of a dozen I.R.S. officials detailed to a task force formed in response to Mr. Kirk’s death on Sept. 10, 2025,” the NYT reports.

As TPM’s Josh Kovensky has reported at length, while the Trump administration ostentatiously turned Kirk’s death into a national day of mourning, it also seized on the assassination as a pretext to criminalize dissent, invent a left-wing terrorism threat that it falsely claimed had international connections, and scrutinize left-wing political and advocacy groups in an effort to intimidate and cow protests.

In the two weeks after Kirk’s death, President Trump designated Antifa as a terrorist organization and signed National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7). In NSPM-7, Trump ordered the IRS commissioner “to ensure that no tax-exempt entities are directly or indirectly financing political violence or domestic terrorism” and to refer such organizations and their officers and employees to the DOJ for investigation and prosecution.

“The memo viewed by The Times is the first window into the work the I.R.S. has actually undertaken to carry out the demands from the White House,” according to the story.

In March of this year, the IRS criminal investigations branch began working with the the task force that was operating out of the FBI headquarters, according to the NYT story. The memo covers work done between March and July. The NYT said it reviewed the first six pages of the eight-page memo. The last two pages, which the newspaper did not see, apparently identified the four targeted groups.

The protests at Delany Hall, the immigration detention center in Newark, New Jersey, have been a particular focus of the task force:

I.R.S. officials reviewed financial information, including subpoenaed Venmo records, about people arrested during those protests, as well as businesses that the officials believed could be funding them. At one point, I.R.S. officials used facial recognition and tattoo analysis databases to help identify individuals, the memo said.

A quick summary of some of the memo’s highlights, as reported by the NYT:

  • In addition to the Delaney Hall protests, the IRS also assisted in the response to the April shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, the May shooting at a mosque in San Diego, and the June UFC event on the White House lawn. It’s not clear from the memo what role the IRS had in the UFC event (five men were charged with allegedly plotting to attack the event).

  • At least four tax-exempt groups were referred to the civil side of the agency, which conducts audits;

  • IRS officials have been assigned to nine grand juries.

The memo is just a glimpse into one discrete operation during one window of time this year, and it alone can’t really provide a clear picture of the scale and scope of the effort to turn political opposition to the Trump administration into criminal conduct. That’s one area where a Democratic Congress could bring new facts to light and begin to back the Trump administration off from its worst excesses.

President Trump brought an ignominious end to the political career of Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) by endorsing the scoundrel Ken Paxton and costing Texas a Senate seat — and now it’s having knock-on effects in the final weeks before Cornyn leaves office.

Cornyn appears to be very much on board with having Ohio native T. Elliot Gaiser — the head of the Trump DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel — installed as a federal judge in Texas, where he has few personal or professional connections.

A coveted federal judgeship going to a non-Texan while bypassing the home state senators’ approved list of potential nominees would be a tough ask by any president under any circumstance (unless you’re Ted Cruz, I guess). But under these circumstances, it’s a lot to expect Cornyn to roll over after getting royally screwed:

Cornyn’s remarks came as Bloomberg reported that last year, early in his tenure at OLC, Gaiser pitched a memo that proposed reviving the 1873 Comstock Act to criminalize the transportation of abortion drugs and related medical supplies.

Then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche rejected Gaiser’s pitch, according to Bloomberg’s sources: “Blanche pushed back by directing him to table the issue due to his worry that Gaiser’s position would amount to a federal abortion ban — an issue the administration had avoided wading into before the midterms …”

In an unusual move, Gaiser contacted Bloomberg directly after it published its story and denied it. “Your story is categorically false, period,” Gaiser said. “I did not push for any nationwide abortion ban.”

Where Have You Found AI Most Useful?

I ask this question with some trepidation. For a number of reasons, I have been slow to take affirmative steps to incorporate AI into my personal and professional lives.

I haven’t activated AI on my Apple devices or integrated it into Google yet. I’ve played around with Claude for maybe two hours over the past six months, and I used Gemini to create a couple of satirical images to make a friend laugh (with mixed results). I’ve not touched ChatGPT, and I haven’t used any of the new personal AI agents like Muse.

But I am curious about AI’s utility and how you’re incorporating it as a tool in your lives and work. I’m also pretty leery of the privacy risks involved — so I’d be interested in hearing where you’re drawing the line on entrusting AI tools with personal or sensitive information.

At this point, I should acknowledge that AI is a dreadfully imprecise term so let me refine what I mean for the purposes of this question. If you’re scientist, engineer, developer, or otherwise use AI at a high technical level, I’m probably not looking for for feedback from you. But even that can be a fuzzy line to draw. For example, a friend who is not a professional coder used AI to code a draftboard for his fantasy baseball team. So the newest AI tools may put some of what we used to think of as technical work within reach of a layperson. Obviously the AI I’m talking about here is a far cry from the frontier work on artificial general intelligence. You get the idea.

Let me try to preempt the emails warning me about the evils of AI or how you’re not using it and will never use it. I get you. My own slow adoption of AI is partly because it gives me pause, too. This has been a new frontier of consumer tech that I’ve been content not to be on the cutting edge of. But it’s pervasiveness at what I’ll call the retail level — quite apart from its role in research and development, core science, and other technical applications — has me prepared to adapt … possibly.

Thanks in advance for your feedback. My contact information is immediately below.
